name: The Motte-and-Bailey
statement: Advance a bold claim, retreat to a modest one when challenged, then quietly reclaim the bold one.
statementAccent: retreat to a modest one when challenged
meaning: The motte-and-bailey is an informal fallacy and argumentative strategy in which a person conflates two positions that share surface similarities: one modest and easy to defend, the motte, and one controversial and hard to defend, the bailey. The arguer advances the controversial bailey, but when it is challenged, retreats to the modest, defensible motte; once the critic concedes the motte, the arguer returns to the controversial bailey as though it had been vindicated. The name comes from a medieval motte-and-bailey castle, with a defensible tower on a mound, the motte, and a larger desirable courtyard, the bailey, to which occupants retreat and return as danger comes and goes. Coined by the philosopher Nicholas Shackel in 2005, it is a form of equivocation exploiting the resemblance between a strong claim and a weak one.
mechanism: The strategy depends on two claims being similar enough on the surface to be swapped, yet different in strength. The arguer occupies the desirable but weakly defensible bailey, the bold, controversial thesis, until it is attacked. Then, rather than defend it, they retreat to the motte, a modest claim that is trivially true and easy to hold, insisting that this is all they meant. The critic, unable to fault the motte, concedes it, at which point the arguer treats the bold thesis as if it too had survived and returns to advancing it. The equivocation lies in trading on the ambiguity between the two positions, substituting one concept for another without the audience noticing, so a defensible claim is used to shelter an indefensible one.

examples.text: Claiming morality is socially constructed, then when pressed retreating to the modest point that moral practices vary by culture, before reasserting that there is no objective morality at all.
Asserting a strong controversial thesis, saying under challenge that only a trivially true version was meant, then later reasserting the strong thesis as established.
Like castle occupants who live in the open bailey but flee to the fortified motte when attacked, the arguer shelters in the defensible claim only when pressed.

variants.name: Concept-swapping equivocation
variants.text: The underlying move of substituting one concept for another that resembles it, so the audience does not notice the claim has changed.

variants.name: The doctrine versus the fallacy
variants.text: Shackel's original motte-and-bailey doctrine, aimed at postmodernist argument, versus the later popular motte-and-bailey fallacy framing in online discourse.

whyItMatters: The motte-and-bailey is an increasingly cited fallacy in analytic philosophy and online discourse, valued for naming a slippery but common rhetorical move: defending a bold claim by hiding behind a modest one. It captures how arguers can seem to win by retreating to the undeniable when challenged and then quietly advancing the contentious thesis again, exploiting the audience's inattention to the switch. Recognising it sharpens debate by forcing arguers to say which claim they are actually defending and to defend the strong version if they wish to assert it.

working.text: distinguish the modest, defensible motte from the bold, controversial bailey the arguer really wants to assert.

working.lead: Pin down what is being defended
working.text: when an arguer retreats under challenge, ask whether they are abandoning the strong claim or merely sheltering to reassert it later.

working.lead: Demand the strong version be defended
working.text: insist that if the controversial bailey is being advanced, it must be defended on its own, not smuggled back after conceding the motte.

limits: The fallacy is the conflation or bait-and-switch between the two claims, exploiting their surface similarity; it is not committed simply by holding a modest position or by clarifying what one means. Defending a modest claim on its own is legitimate, and genuinely retracting a strong claim in favour of a weaker one is honest, not fallacious; the fault requires the strategic switching back to the controversial claim. Diagnosing it can be contestable, since an arguer may sincerely have meant only the modest claim. Shackel's original coinage was the motte-and-bailey doctrine aimed at postmodernism, with the fallacy framing and wide use popularised later, so the label spans a scholarly origin and a looser online usage.
misreadings: The motte-and-bailey is not merely holding a defensible position; it is the strategic conflation of a modest claim with a controversial one, retreating to the former under fire and returning to the latter when safe. Clarifying or genuinely retracting a claim is not the fallacy, which requires the switch back to the strong thesis. And it is a form of equivocation, a concept-swap the audience does not notice, so it is not simply inconsistency but a deliberate exploitation of the resemblance between the two claims.
origin: Coined by the philosopher Nicholas Shackel in his 2005 paper The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology in Metaphilosophy, originally as the motte-and-bailey doctrine, with the fallacy framing later popularised in online discourse.
